critique.good: Host, role, zone, CPU and status values stay on one line, making ordinary rows compact and comparisons easy. The wider Notes column gives the long operational explanation a readable measure.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through Status and leaves Notes offscreen, separating the degraded indicator from its explanation. The tall note row also creates a large vertical gap before the remaining servers.
critique.cause: The first four columns consume 319px, so the 88px Status column extends beyond the viewport; the 180px Notes column begins farther right. Its long content determines the degraded row's height.

critique.good: All headers stay intact, and Status fits within the initial viewport. Role, CPU and status values are easy to compare without mid-word splits.
critique.problems: Host identifiers and zones break across lines, making routine rows much taller and harder to scan. Notes starts beyond the viewport and is so narrow that the degraded row becomes exceptionally tall.
critique.cause: The 70px Host and 60px Zone columns force wraps at hyphens. Notes has only 64px of content width, producing a 29-line note.

critique.good: The whole table fits in the viewport, so status and its note are visible together without horizontal scrolling.
critique.problems: Several headers, identifiers, roles and status values split inside words. This damages the column hierarchy and makes ordinary rows difficult to scan, while the long note still produces a very tall row.
critique.cause: The 55px Host, 58px Role, 43px CPU and 66px Status widths leave too little content space for their longest words. The 82px Notes column leaves only 61px for text.

critique.good: Role, CPU and status are easy to compare, and the wider notes column limits the height of the exceptional row. Words remain intact.
critique.problems: Host identifiers and zones wrap in ordinary rows, making the inventory taller and slowing identification. Notes start beyond the viewport, so the explanation for the degraded server is hidden initially.
critique.cause: Host is 70px wide, leaving only 49px for text; Zone is 80px, leaving 59px. The first five columns total 371px, so Notes begins beyond the 360px viewport.

critique.good: Role, CPU and status remain readable, and the notes column begins near the viewport edge. The table requires less horizontal scrolling than r1A.
critique.problems: Zones break across three lines and host identifiers still wrap, giving every ordinary row excessive height. The long note creates a large blank area across the rest of its row.
critique.cause: Zone has only 39px of text width and Host only 49px. Notes is reduced to 180px, causing the long note to wrap more than in r1A.

critique.good: The smaller overflow reduces horizontal scrolling, while role, CPU and status remain legible.
critique.problems: Three-line zones and wrapped host identifiers make ordinary rows tall. The narrow note becomes a very long column of text, leaving a conspicuous expanse of empty cells and making the degraded row hard to read as a unit.
critique.cause: Zone is 60px and Host is 70px; Notes is only 120px, leaving 99px for text and producing 17 lines in the longest cell.

critique.good: Host, role, zone, CPU and status values remain intact, making the ordinary rows compact and easy to compare. The wider Notes column limits the height of the exceptional row.
critique.problems: The degraded row still creates a large blank area across the other columns. Status is cut by the initial viewport edge and Notes requires horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 240px Notes column wraps the long note to seven lines; the first four columns already occupy 319px, leaving only 41px of the 88px Status column in view.

critique.good: Identifiers, roles, CPU values and status words stay intact, and the table is 40px narrower than r2A.
critique.problems: Every zone wraps onto two lines, making all ordinary rows taller and weakening the rhythm of the inventory. Status remains partly outside the initial viewport, and the long note makes the exceptional row taller than in r2A.
critique.cause: Zone is reduced to 80px, leaving 59px for a value that needs 79px on one line. Notes is reduced to 220px, producing eight lines in the long note.

critique.good: The narrower table reduces horizontal scrolling and brings more of Status into the initial viewport.
critique.problems: Zone names fragment over three lines in every row, the degraded status splits mid-word, and the long note becomes taller. The resulting repeated row height and broken status make scanning harder.
critique.cause: The 60px Zone column leaves only 39px for text; the 80px Status column leaves 59px for a word needing 67px. The 200px Notes column wraps the long note to nine lines.

understanding.purpose: An inventory for checking server identity, function, location, capacity, health and operational notes.
understanding.reading: Readers scan hosts and compare roles, zones, CPU counts and status; the degraded server’s long note calls for closer reading across that row.
groups: Host and Role identify each server and its function.
Zone and CPU describe placement and capacity for comparison across servers.
Status and Notes pair the health indicator with its operational explanation.
keep_intact: Host identifiers and zone names, so servers and locations are easy to distinguish.
CPU values and status words, so comparisons remain quick and unambiguous.
may_wrap: The long note can wrap at word boundaries; its row is already taller than the others.
Zone names may wrap at natural hyphen boundaries if space is constrained.

bad.why: Host identifiers wrap and every zone breaks across three lines, making ordinary rows tall and harder to scan.
The same repeated identifier wrapping is compounded by a 17-line note, producing an exceptionally tall table.
Every zone wraps, making all ordinary rows taller even though the table still requires substantial horizontal scrolling.
Every zone breaks across three lines, and the important status word ‘degraded’ splits mid-word.
Every zone wraps and enlarges ordinary rows, while the wider notes column adds substantial scrolling.

final.rationale: r2A keeps host names and zones intact and gives the six ordinary rows a compact, consistent rhythm. Its notes column contains the exceptional long entry in seven lines without making the table as wide as r3A. Status is only partly visible at the initial viewport edge, and the note requires horizontal scrolling; that is a meaningful cost for an inventory where the degraded row matters.

general: Keep identifiers intact when readers need to recognize and compare them across rows.
Judge horizontal scrolling against repeated wrapping: saving width can make every row harder to scan.
Size an exceptional prose column with its effect on the whole row and table in mind.
specific: A 100px zone column preserves the full zone values and reduces six ordinary rows to one line.
One long note drives the exceptional row height, while the remaining notes are sparse.
At the preferred widths, the initial viewport cuts through Status and leaves Notes offscreen.

final.tradeoffs: r3A shortens the long note to five lines but requires 80px more horizontal scrolling than r2A. r3B reduces scrolling by 60px but stretches the exceptional row to 11 lines.
final.uncertain: A designer who prioritizes keeping Status fully visible at first sight might accept more wrapping or choose a different allocation. The ranges are approximate, independent adjustments around r2A, not browser-tested guarantees; simultaneous changes can alter the balance and scrolling cost.

A.why: Everything fits in the viewport, but hostnames, roles, statuses and the note split into fragments. The exceptionally tall row makes the inventory difficult to scan.

B.why: Host, role, zone and CPU remain intact, but status is cut by the viewport edge and the note requires horizontal scrolling. The long row leaves substantial empty space in the other columns.

C.why: Status fits at first sight, but hostnames and zones wrap repeatedly, and the narrow note creates a very tall row. The note also lies beyond the viewport.

D.why: The inventory fields remain intact and the long row is shorter than in B. Status is still cut by the viewport edge, and the note requires scrolling.

E.why: Status fits in the viewport, but several hostnames and all zones wrap, weakening comparisons. The long note is offscreen and creates a large gap between inventory rows.

F.why: The inventory fields remain intact and the long row is the shortest of the scrolling layouts, making the rows easier to compare. Status is cut at the viewport edge and the note requires scrolling.

reviews.unsure: The supplied images are cropped at the right edge, so the full widths and wrapping of the Notes columns are not visible. That makes the horizontal scrolling cost, and the comparison between B, D and F, uncertain.

A.why: Host, role, zone and CPU values scan cleanly, but status is cut by the viewport edge and the long note makes one row unusually tall. Reading the note requires horizontal scrolling.

B.why: The table fits the viewport, but hostnames, roles, zones, status labels and the note are split into fragments. The long note creates an extremely tall row and makes comparison difficult.

C.why: The visible inventory values stay intact and the long-note row is relatively compact. Status falls across the viewport edge, and the note requires horizontal scrolling.

D.why: Status fits initially, but hostnames and zones wrap repeatedly. The narrow note column produces a very tall row while still requiring scrolling to read it.

E.why: The visible inventory values stay intact and the long-note row is moderately compact. Status is cut by the viewport edge, and the note lies beyond it.
